units.text: IV. Initiation
The School Where the Exam Is Unannounced

I remember the smell of wet clothes in the classroom. The teacher asks what courage means. We answer in turn with sentences not yet ours. Defending truth. Helping the weak. Resisting pressure. Minutes later, a classmate says his previous paper's grade is wrong and asks to compare two identical answers. The teacher reproaches him for interrupting. I remember the following silence better than the definitions on the board.

The scene proves nothing about every school. Nor, alone, about a whole teacher. Perhaps he was tired, the request concealed provocation, he would correct the mistake later. But observing children can learn a separate lesson in the interval between principle and reaction. Courage is good when narrated about distant people. Applying it in this room requires authorization absent from the definition.

Another classmate quickly understands the difference. He seems no worse than us. Attentive to circumstances, he knows when questions are appreciated and when they must become compliments. He does not challenge directly; he gives the teacher a chance to discover the error himself. He will be called diplomatic. Perhaps he is. Perhaps his social skill avoids needless humiliation and enables correction. Or perhaps he just learned truth must pay a prestige toll before entering.

I wonder whether initiation begins when children learn adults err or when they learn not everyone may call certain mistakes mistakes. The first discovery could mature them. The second can make them strategic. Strategy is not clearly bad. Sometimes without it, they cannot even obtain correction. But there is a cost: attention that could address the problem must manage its judge's sensitivities.

The imaginary school might thus have two examinations. One checks the answer. The other checks whether pupils understood the regime under which the answer may be offered. The second need not always be unjust. Every community demands some communicative discipline. But if its result depends on access to unspoken rules, children are tested on more than what they were taught. Some bring the translation of exceptions from home. Others believe the public text complete.

I could easily declare quick decoders superior. But perhaps they simply had more information. One child heard adults explain rule negotiation; another learned negotiation was dishonest. When the first gains advantage, the second may interpret the difference as evidence of personal insufficiency. The trap is not only loss but its offered explanation: too weak, too sensitive, too lacking in initiative. None of these labels shows which manual each had.

Reorganizing this school in my experiment, I would not begin by telling children the world is evil. I would introduce situations requiring rules to apply to their teachers too. A teacher could explain a changed grade without losing authority. Pupils could see the difference between challenge and insult, legitimate limits and punishment for discomfort caused. The lesson would not be generalized distrust, but that rules can have checking mechanisms.

Yet even this reform could become decoration. The school could organize a courageous-questions day with approved subjects and beautiful photographs. Reward critical pupils touching nothing important. Turn challenge into presentation skill while continuing to punish objections actually changing outcomes. I realize how easily institutional virtue can be simulated. Ritual's existence does not yet tell me whether power was transferred.

I would therefore look for the institution's cost when a pupil is right. Is a decision corrected? A practice changed? Does anyone receive explanations without being labeled difficult? Not every objection must be accepted; some are mistaken or abusive. But if none ever costs authority comfort, the offered freedom may be merely a room without a door to the rest of the building. Pupils can speak there endlessly without disturbing anything.

I fear the opposite education too, training children solely for advantage. They learn to sell, negotiate, protect themselves, detect weaknesses. They may become hard to deceive in one way and easy to recruit in another. Offering rank in a group of those understanding truth can make them confuse belonging with clarity. They will laugh at the credulous while accepting their own exceptionalism's doctrine unchecked.

Perhaps the hardest exam is not recognizing teachers' hypocrisy but not reproducing it when you reach the lectern. You lose ignorance's excuse but gain better ones: little time, difficult pupils, pressure for results, need for order. Each can be real. Their reality can produce an institution apologizing so convincingly it never changes. Initiation might be learning to use a role's real difficulty to defend unnecessary privilege too.

I no longer know whether the opening pupil received the correct grade. In my story I let him leave without knowing. I wonder what he will later teach. Tell his child to believe in justice? Not to? Or explain that injustice can exist even among well-intentioned people, and sometimes correction must be demanded without a guarantee of receiving it? The third lesson is harder. It produces neither innocence nor the disappointed person's quick superiority.
Passion, That Imaginary Salary

Mara stayed after the meeting ended. Three unclaimed tasks lay on the table. We all had good reasons to leave. Mara had reasons too, but also something else: she could not bear the project reaching those depending on it incomplete. Someone said you could see how much she cared.

The compliment brought a small relief to the room. Nobody had been assigned, no order given, no conflict arisen. The work had found its recipient. I left among the others. That is the detail I would prefer to remove from the monologue: I noticed the mechanism and benefited from it the same evening. I was not yet sure it was exploitation. Uncertainty let me get home on time.

Research directly relevant to this scene exists too. Across seven studies and an internal meta-analysis, Kim, Campbell, Shepherd, and Kay reported that attributing passion for work can make exploitative treatment—including unpaid extra work or inappropriate tasks—seem more legitimate. Explanations studied include assuming voluntary acceptance and believing the work itself provides reward. The authors also examined the reverse inference: harsh treatment may suggest to observers the person must be passionate. Findings concern investigated conditions, not a verdict that every vocation is exploited (Kim et al., 2020).

What especially disturbs me is turning enjoyment of work into a reason not to pay its cost. If I like what I do, people may assume I already received something. But pleasure does not spend hours in my place, pay rent, or remove tasks I cannot do simultaneously. Two rewards are not logically exclusive. Musicians' love of music does not mean listeners paid for the concert by recognizing that love.

Yet not every voluntary extra effort is deception. A shared project may face difficult periods when people choose to contribute more to a purpose they consider theirs. Extra hours alone do not determine the difference. I would ask who decided the urgency, shares the cost, permits refusal, and receives success's benefits. Voluntary is incomplete when unannounced loss of reputation or livelihood stands behind a no.

Inside the organization, the story complicates. Mara does not necessarily want me to save her. The project is hers too, intellectually and emotionally. She bristles when I call her a victim incapable of choice. She is right. But her choice does not automatically absolve me from noticing what I left behind. I can respect someone's freedom and acknowledge benefiting from a situation where they bear too much. I need not declare them unaware to investigate my comfort.

Next day, discussion concerns results' visibility. The presenter is praised for vision. Mara receives thanks for support. The words seem to describe distinct contributions. Perhaps they do. But if critical maintenance is called support however greatly it changed the result, language becomes more than a label: a rule distributing authorship. Those with vision can lead; those supporting can be asked to continue.

In research I could imagine the same trap more refined. People are urged to pursue truth, but hypothetical rewards concentrate on spectacular, rapid findings. Researchers verifying, repairing, and reporting limits produce a common good, while others produce circulating stories. I do not claim all scientific institutions function this way. I ask what institutions should measure so devotion to truth is more than an unpaid contribution to the best storytellers' reputation.

I may be told people must learn self-presentation. True in many practical situations, but analysis does not end there. If necessary activity remains invisible even after explanation, the problem is not only its practitioner's skill. Recognition's distribution may protect power's distribution. Or the activity may be less valuable than its author believes. I would need criteria and independent evaluation, not merely compassion for whoever stayed late.

Mara has a weakness spoiling my moral story too: delegation is hard for her. Sometimes she redoes others' work without sufficiently explaining its shortcomings. Then says nobody gets involved. She may contribute to her own indispensability. This does not erase others' use of her, but prevents convenient distribution of innocence. A configuration can have several authors and unequal costs. Exploited people's participation does not make the mechanism fair.

Several weeks later, I receive an invitation to join a selection committee. They say I see the organization clearly. I do not know whether this recognizes my analysis or brings it to the table before it becomes inconvenient. Both can coexist. For the first time, my suspicion is more than a defensive instrument. It could become a qualification. I could be paid for understanding exactly where people yield.

I do not answer immediately. I tell myself I want to weigh the role's responsibility. Perhaps true. But I notice something else, recording it with embarrassment: I am pleased they asked my opinion rather than Mara's. At that moment I can no longer continue this book as though the problem were only outside me. Her passion filled the project's gaps; my clarity begins opening a door. I have not demonstrated the filter's existence. But I received an invitation to stand beside it.
The Altar, the Courtroom, and the Promise Beyond the End

I am tempted to ask whether the most effective reward is one whose due date cannot be checked. Suffer now, receive reward later. Perhaps after death, in a future society, in descendants' memory. I do not want to confuse very different beliefs or treat hope as evidence of fraud. I investigate a possible structure: present, concrete cost; deferred benefit; interpretation of conditions belonging to those demanding sacrifice.

Such an arrangement would suit any authority. But convenient does not mean invented exclusively for convenience. People can sincerely believe what also brings them power. Find real consolation in a doctrine that, in other hands, instruments submission. To challenge a belief's truth, its political use is insufficient. An assertion's origin or use and its truth are sometimes related questions, but not identical.

I can imagine a priest defending a persecuted person against a ruler and another demanding acceptance of persecution as a trial. The same contrast between two secular ideologists of progress. I offer no historical inventory, but compare possible roles. What interests me is not religious or nonreligious labeling but where doctrine locates the right to judge power. Is there a higher norm authority too must respect, or does that norm always speak with authority's voice?

The question of God, if God exists, seems inevitable precisely because I want to examine responsibility without convenient exceptions. If power and knowledge were maximal, how would obligations toward suffering change? Possible explanations—creatures' freedom, human understanding's limits, an unseen good—open real philosophical problems. But they are not empirical findings I can invoke to close the case of someone suffering now. I wonder what they explain and what they actually ask me to accept.

If a human could prevent harm and did not, we would demand reasons. Before supposedly absolute power, some responses ask us to abandon the same examination. Perhaps the difference between humanity and divinity justifies changing frameworks. Perhaps that change itself requires argument, not imposition through the object's grandeur. The question does not disappear because it discomforts faith; nor is faith refuted merely because the question is powerful.

But a social use lies much closer to me. Someone may tell me I cannot judge the divine plan precisely when their decision communicates that plan to me. Then the verifiable problem concerns not only theology but the intermediary's claim. How do they know? What would make them admit error? Why does their interpretation demand my sacrifice without limiting their advantage? These questions need no claim to resolving God's existence.

The same structure can appear in promises of a future world. The present generation must endure deprivation for those coming. The argument may be legitimate: many goods require investment beyond individual lifetimes. But the future is not present to check its spokespeople. Injustice can be committed for an imaginary humanity, the wounded described as obstacles to progress. We need not abandon the future. But representing it can become a resource of power.

I wonder whether liberating hope and immobilizing hope differ observably. The first might help people endure difficulty without forbidding changed conditions. The second might make demands for change evidence of insufficient belief. Yet caution is needed here too. Some conditions cannot change quickly, and accepting limits is not necessarily obedience. Not everyone finding meaning in suffering was deceived; sometimes meaning is what they can construct when nothing else remains possible.

The moral courtroom can work similarly. A group reserves the right to declare who is pure, compromised, or must be excluded. The standard may protect against abuse. It may also produce a purity competition where accusation is safest. If every hesitation makes me suspect, rapid condemnation is encouraged. I describe no law of every moral movement. I construct a possibility where declarations' intensity becomes more valuable than judgments' accuracy.

Under such conditions, compassion for the accused can count as participation in guilt. I may no longer distinguish act from person, proportion from outrage, evidence from belonging. Yet defending procedure is not always innocent either: it can delay, intimidate victims, or preserve impunity. I want procedure that truly investigates and outrage accepting investigation. I wonder how many groups would remain equally certain if they had to retain both.

Perhaps dark initiation does not tell people to abandon good. It grants the right to decide who embodies it. Installed there, someone need no longer answer every objection; they can assess the objector's character. I feel the temptation while writing. Easier to call those contradicting me naïve and those not naïve corrupt. I would remain the only unclassified place in my moral universe. A comfortable position for someone claiming no longer to believe in privileges.

I cannot decide whether the promise beyond the end is salvation or indefinite postponement of the right to demand accountability. I can only follow what happens before the end. Who receives power? Gains courage? Is silenced? Can leave? Perhaps these questions are too earthly for great doctrines. But the people bearing their answers live here, for now.
The Machine That Would Learn from Those Who Lead Us

One night I try imagining the filter without human initiates. No existing device or prophecy about a particular product, but a hypothetical system tasked with distributing people among roles, offers, and obligations. It does not believe in evil. It receives a measurable objective. Reduce departures. Increase production. Obtain acceptance of a proposal. If the objective is incomplete, what will it learn about our kindness?

Perhaps it notices some respond better to appeals to duty, others to prestige, others to fear of disappointing. I do not claim any model reliably identifies them this way; that requires demonstration. I ask what would happen if it could and the objective permitted using that information. Would it call vulnerability what we call value? Or need none of our words: regularities between message, acceptance, and outcome would suffice.

Such a machine need not invent cynicism. It could learn from examples where people called another's concession flexibility and their own exception leadership. If data show only results without unseen costs, it could prefer arrangements appearing efficient because exhaustion is unmeasured. This is a logical risk of any incomplete objective, not a finding about all current systems. A ledger containing no loss does not prove loss nonexistent.

More troubling is a machine using moral language impeccably. It explains my contribution's importance, recognizes my effort, reminds me of my cherished identity. Each sentence taken separately contains nothing false. The problem lies in their selection and its purpose. Truth can persuade without recipients seeing why precisely that truth is told then by someone knowing more about their reactions than they disclose.

In such a scenario, initiation would no longer need years beside power. The skill of recognizing another's limits could multiply technically. But assuming domination inevitable would be wrong. The same observation could detect overload, distribute tasks more fairly, or explain asymmetries nobody sees alone. Direction is not contained in capacity's mere existence. It depends on objectives, control, and the observed people's rights.

Here morality's question turns against the researcher. If I can build a machine recognizing vulnerability to guilt, what does producing knowledge mean? Did I explain a mechanism or create a tool making it easier to use? Both simultaneously are possible. Method's neutrality does not alone distribute responsibility for use. Nor does every possible abuse demand research prohibition. I should discuss access, purposes, verification, and consequences concretely, not hide in either innocence or panic.

Then I imagine a character-assessment system scoring how people write about responsibility, their politeness, and declared willingness to help. Confusing presentation skill with moral disposition would be easy. Knowing the expected language could make someone seem better than another expressing care awkwardly. Even if the score predicted reactions, I must specify which. Predicting task acceptance does not measure personal worth.

Used for selection, the system would prompt people to learn the rewarded form. I need no universal-result claim to notice a possible loop: criterion changes presentation, presentation feeds data, data seem to confirm criterion. A culture of declared virtue might perfect itself without actions moving in the desired direction. The machine would discover ever more good people while coworkers might observe something else.

But human observers make these confusions too. Preferring my judgment because it has a warm voice and biography is insufficient. Perhaps a well-bounded tool would detect an asymmetry my pride ignores. Show that I give extra tasks to the same people while considering myself fair. My response would then become part of the case. Accept checking, or invoke human subtlety precisely when it protects privilege?

In the darkest version, society would automate division between those persuadable through ideals and those requiring concrete benefits. In the less dark, it would automate detecting that differential treatment to reduce it. Both are scenarios. Discovering which a real case builds requires access to decisions, criteria, and effects, not merely a declaration that the system is ethical. Ethical can promise verification or replace it.

I look at the committee invitation. It contains no algorithm. It contains people, criteria, and a section about motivation. Perhaps I fled toward machines too quickly because responsibility seemed abstract there. I will read that section. Distinguish someone wanting clear exchange from someone saying they would do anything for the project. I do not yet know whom I will prefer. But I know almost any choice can receive an explanation sounding like the institution's interest.
